content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper proposes an approach for improving pretrained models of source code for generating better code, if the input includes test cases. Given a pretrained model of code, a natural language (NL) description of the problem, and a few input-output examples, the authors use a Monte-Carlo tree search (MCTS)-based algorithm to generate code that satisfies the input-output examples, instead of just sampling / using beam search and "hoping" that the generated code will satisfy the input-output examples (="pass the tests").
The idea is demonstrated on the APPS dataset, across GPT-2-1.5B and GPT-Neo-2.7B models, where the model passes more tests than the standard approaches of beam search or sampling + post-filtering.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths
+ The problem is important and has a broad interest.
+ The idea is interesting conceptually and shows improved results.
+ The idea of treating code generation as an RL problem, where input-output pairs provide the reward, is novel and related to much work in program synthesis.

### Weaknesses
- **Usability** - I am finding it hard to see how the approach can be usable in realistic settings. This severe limitation is not explicitly mentioned, and is clear only to readers who are very familiar with the field and its datasets: while the paper places itself besides general models of code such as Codex,  CodeBERT, CodeT5 etc., the proposed approach is actually much more limited than them, and does not "play the same game". While Codex (for example) is only **tested** on executable test-cases to measure its execution accuracy, the proposed approach **requires training** on the input-output pairs. Further, not only that it requires input-output pairs at training time, at test time it can only be applied to examples that have input-output pairs as well.

In contrast, all other models (Codex,  CodeBERT, CodeT5 etc.) can be applied (at test time) to inputs that do not have input-output pairs, and this way they can serve as general code-completion / code-generation / bug-detection assistants.
The proposed approach kind of "overfits" on the existing benchmarks, while losing usability on the realistic tasks that these benchmarks are meant to be a proxy of.
How do the authors see the proposed model to be useful in real life? In which settings and tasks do we expect the user to provide both a natural language intent *and* test cases?

- **Clarity** - discussed in the next section.

content.title: Response to Reviewer FcyD
content.comment:
Dear Reviewer FcyD,

We thank the reviewer for the comments and questions.

**Q1 and Q2. Rationale of using test cases.**
> 1. How do the authors see the proposed model to be useful in real life? In which settings and tasks?
> 2. "We assume that the agent has access to a set of test cases" - while this is the assumption of traditional "programming by example ..." approaches, in which modern realistic settings is this a reasonable assumption?

We would like to emphasize that test cases are a unique feature that makes programming languages different from natural languages. Unlike natural language generation, where the goal is to generate sequences that resemble human languages, programming language generation tasks aim to generate programs that can successfully run and output the correct solutions. Even for one of the most capable code-generation Transformers, Codex, validating the generated programs by executing on a set of test cases can dramatically improve its performance (Table A). Therefore, **test cases are crucial to validate the correctness of the programs**. Nonetheless, it remains an open and challenging problem on how to make use of the provided test cases. Our paper aims to provide a novel decoding algorithm (PG-TD) to fill this gap.

We agree with the reviewer that **"where the test cases come from"** is an important question that we need to answer to make our work more practically useful. There has been recent work on generating useful test cases for solving coding challenges. For example, AlphaCode [1] train an LLM-based test input generation model that generates test cases from natural language descriptions. They execute the generated programs on these test cases for clustering and filtering out low-quality programs. We evaluated our methods on the CodeContest dataset released in [1] （see table 1 of the main paper). In this dataset, **the majority of the test cases we used as public test cases are automatically generated**. This confirms that our framework works with automatically-generated test cases. 

Another real-world use case of our algorithm is code translation. The goal of code translation is to translate a script from one programming language to another. In this problem, automatically generated test cases are used to determine if the translated codes are correct [2]. The automatic test case generation problem is well-explored in this problem and **there exist tools like EvoSuite, Jtest, etc. that can generate useful test cases that can be used by PG-TD.** We conducted code translation experiments in the following table. We use TransCoder-ST [2] as the backbone Transformer, and compare beam search with PG-TD. In PG-TD, it uses EvoSuite to generate *public test cases*, and use the pass rates on them as rewards in the generation process. The translated codes are evaluated on a set of private test cases. We can see that in this problem, PG-TD also outperforms the beam search algorithm.

Table E. Pass rates of applying our method for code translation, where test cases are automatically generated. The baseline results are copied from the original paper. 
|  | Python -> Java | CPP -> Java |
| -------- | -------- | -------- |
| Beam Search         | 58.2     | 68.0     |
| PG-TD     | 63.5     | 70.6     |

Therefore, **our PG-TD algorithm can be useful in multiple real-world coding tasks such as coding problem solving [1] and code translation [2].** We will add discussions on test cases and summarize related work to the final version of the paper.

[1]. Yujia Li, David Choi, Junyoung Chung, Nate Kushman, Julian Schrittwieser, R ́emi Leblond, Tom Eccles, James Keeling, Felix Gimeno, and Agustin Dal Lago. Competition-Level Code Generation with AlphaCode. arXiv preprint arXiv:2203.07814, 2022.

[2]. Baptiste Roziere, Jie M Zhang, Francois Charton, Mark Harman, Gabriel Synnaeve, and Guillaume Lample. Leveraging automated unit tests for unsupervised code translation. In International Conference on Learning Representations, 2022.


**Q3. Qualitative and quantitative results using Codex.**
> 3. I would like to see more motivating cases that show examples that the standard transformer could not solve at all, and were only solved thanks to PG-TD.

We have added a new example where the Codex model fails to solve the problem using beam search, but successfully solves the problem (pass rate = 1) using PG-TD. Please see Fig. 15 in the revision.

content.title: Response to Reviewer FcyD
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the follow-up questions and insightful feedback.

> I did not read the CodeContest dataset paper, but I am assuming that these test cases were generated after the code existed? So why is it meaningful to generate code given these test cases? Otherwise, how could the test cases be generated before the code was written?
> In other words, it seems like the authors claim that "test case generation is a solved problem". I don't think this is true, and it requires more empirical evidence and end-to-end evaluation.

We could use a machine learning model to generate not only *codes*, but also *test cases* from natural language descriptions. Indeed, the AlphaCode paper [1] has shown promising results. In their CodeContests dataset, **the test case inputs are automatically generated from the natural language descriptions of the problems**. As they have stated in the paper,  *"We trained a separate test input generation model, using the same architecture as our main models, and initialised from the same GitHub pre-trained checkpoint. **This model was trained to predict test inputs from problem descriptions**, using example, hidden, and generated test inputs as training data. After training, this model was used to create new test inputs for unseen problems."* (Page 13 of Section 4.6 Clustering in [1])

It would be indeed more challenging to automatically generates *both the input and output* of test cases. However, if we use a neural network that generates test cases used by our algorithm, we could use a co-training or GAN-like training diagram to improve both the performance of our code generation algorithm and the quality of the test cases. We will leave it for future work.

We'd also like to clarify that we do **not** believe that test case generation is a solved problem. As we have reviewed in the related work section, **many works in the code generation literature rely on test cases for code generation [1-5].** We agree with the reviewer that it remains an important question how to automatically generate useful test cases (input, output pairs) to help algorithms that use test cases like ours. 

> Of course, test cases are crucial. But as I asked, how do the authors expect the proposed model to be useful in real life?

Our proposed model is useful in the following ways.

First, we can **train a separate model to predict test cases from natural language problem descriptions**. We have shown empirical evidence that when evaluated on CodeContests (in Table 1), our algorithm shows significant improvement over beam search using test cases where the test inputs are automatically generated. 

Second, we want to emphasize that **our method does not require many test cases**. We have shown in Table 7 in the appendix that even with one or two public test cases, our method shows significant improvement over the beam search baseline. If a human user is willing to specify *one or two* test cases, that can significantly help our algorithm. Although, as we expect, more test cases can further help our algorithm.

Lastly, **our algorithm is versatile and can be used for other code generation problems**. In Table E, we show that our algorithm can be applied to a code translation task and has a better performance than the beam search baseline. In this problem, the code in the source language already exists so it is easier to automatically generate test cases.

To summarize, although the important problem of automatic test generation is beyond the scope of our paper, we could benefit from automatically-generated test cases like in [1] or use a small number of human-designed test cases if available. Please don’t hesitate to let us know if there are any additional clarifications that we can offer. We would love to convince you of the merits of the paper. We appreciate your suggestions. Thanks!


[1]. Yujia Li, David Choi, Junyoung Chung, Nate Kushman, Julian Schrittwieser, R ́emi Leblond, Tom Eccles, James Keeling, Felix Gimeno, and Agustin Dal Lago. Competition-Level Code Generation with AlphaCode. arXiv preprint arXiv:2203.07814, 2022.

[2]. Bunel, Rudy, et al. "Leveraging grammar and reinforcement learning for neural program synthesis." arXiv preprint arXiv:1805.04276 (2018).

[3]. Chen, Xinyun, Chang Liu, and Dawn Song. "Execution-guided neural program synthesis." International Conference on Learning Representations. 2018.

[4]. Chen, Xinyun, Dawn Song, and Yuandong Tian. "Latent execution for neural program synthesis beyond domain-specific languages." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 34 (2021): 22196-22208.

[5]. Xu, Yifan, et al. "Neural Program Synthesis By Self-Learning." arXiv preprint arXiv:1910.05865 (2019).

content.title: Response to Reviewer FcyD
content.comment:
We would like to emphasize that our PG-TD algorithm can work with either human-specified test cases or automatically-generated ones (which we will show in this response). If a human user is willing to specify even a small number of test cases, our algorithm can perform dramatically better than beam search (Table 7 in the paper).
 
When human-specified test cases are not available, our algorithm can still rely on automatically-generated test cases. We agree with the reviewer that it is an important and challenging problem to generate useful test cases for code generation. In this response, we provide additional experimental results to answer the following questions.
1. *Can large language models (like Codex) generate correct test cases?*
2. *Can the PG-TD algorithm take advantage of the automatically-generated test cases to generate better programs?*

We first follow [1] to use the Codex model and evaluate the code generation algorithms on the HumanEval dataset [2]. We adopt the same procedure as [1] to automatically generate test cases. Concretely, we use a prompt that includes the natural language description of the problem and an `assert` statement at the end of the prompt. We also **removed the example input, output pairs in the problem description** to avoid the Transformer from directly copying the test cases in the problem description. The following is an example of the prompt for test case generation.
```
from typing import List

def has_close_elements(numbers: List[float], threshold: float) -> bool:
    """ Check if in given list of numbers, are any two numbers closer to each other than
    given threshold.
    """
    pass

# check the correctness of has_close_elements
def check(candidate):
    assert candidate
```

**Does Codex generate correct test cases?** In the HumanEval dataset, the generated solutions are evaluated by the test script by calling the `check` function. So we use the strict accuracy (pass@1) metric that counts the percentage of the problems where the generated solutions pass the `check` function.

To evaluate the quality of the automatically-generated test cases, we compute the strict accuracies of the *sample solutions* (correct solutions written by human programmers) on them. The strict accuracies of the sample solutions on the *ground-truth test cases* should be 100%. We **evaluate the sample solutions on the automatically-generated test cases and find the corresponding strict accuracy is 72.56%** over the whole HumanEval dataset, which confirms that the automatically-generated test cases are mostly correct.

**Can PG-TD take advantage of the automatically-generated test cases?** Since OpenAI restricts the frequency of using the Codex model, we have been striving to run the PG-TD algorithm using the automatically-generated test cases to verify the test cases' effectiveness. We report the average strict accuracy of the generated programs on a subset of HumanEval problems in Table H. We can confirm that the strict accuracy is higher for PG-TD as it uses high-quality automatically-generated test cases to verify the generated programs. We are currently running experiments on more problems to make the results more comprehensive.

We also find the pattern that using beam search, the Codex model tends to generate redundant codes, which eventually make the program fail to execute. This issue is resolved by PG-TD, which verifies the generated programs using the automatically-generated test cases.

Table H. Comparison between beam search and TG-PD using automatically-generated test cases, using the Codex model and evaluated on the first 20 problems in the HumanEval dataset.
|             | Strict Accuracy (%) |
| ----------- | --------- |
| Beam Search | 30.0      |
| PG-TD (using auto-generated test cases) | 50.0          |


[1] *Anonymous authors*. CodeT: Code Generation with Generated Tests
https://openreview.net/pdf?id=ktrw68Cmu9c

[2] Chen, Mark, et al. "Evaluating large language models trained on code." arXiv preprint arXiv:2107.03374 (2021).

We wish that our response has addressed your concerns, and turns your assessment to the positive side. If you have any questions, please feel free to let us know during the rebuttal window. We appreciate your suggestions and comments! Thank you!

Best,

Authors

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes using a (MCTS-inspired) heuristic planning algorithm to guide the decoding process of a pre-trained code-generation transformer, for the specific task of test-case-guided competitive programming. At a high level, the proposed decoding strategy maintains a tree of prefixes, conducts beam-search-based "rollouts" and evaluates them on test cases to assess quality of these prefixes, then uses this information to determine which tree nodes to continue exploring. (I believe that the proposed method is deterministic, in contrast to MCTS which is stochastic by design.)

Since beam search and greedy decoding already involve expanding a tree of tokens, the authors introduce caching mechanisms to make their proposed planner more efficient: they cache the tree structure generated during beam search and re-use it when expanding nodes for MCTS, and (when using greedy rollouts) they cache the greedy decoding output for any given prefix and re-use it when expanding the nodes along an already-explored trajectory.

The authors compare their approach to beam search, sample-and-filter approaches (such as the one used by AlphaCode), and the SMCG-TD decoding strategy proposed by Ellis et al. (2019). They argue that their decoding strategy outperforms these other strategies, although some of this may be due to the particular hyperparameters they used; for a fixed number of generated programs or fixed computation time their approach seems to perform fairly similarly to SMCG-TD.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

- Integrating LM generation with MCTS is a good idea, allowing the search process to focus on prefixes with a higher chance of producing good programs.
- The ability of their approach to cache and reuse outputs from the beam-search rollouts means the proposed strategy can be implemented fairly efficiently.
- Their method seems to slightly outperform baseline methods given a fixed runtime budget, without needing to retrain the transformer model.

Weaknesses:

- **(mostly resolved in new revision)** Although the authors refer to their planning algorithm as MCTS, the "Monte Carlo" aspect appears to be missing. The proposed approach is deterministic: it selects actions based on the most-likely tokens following a prefix, and computes "rollouts" using either beam search or greedy decoding.
  - The algorithm thus seems more like a heuristic best-first search than MCTS. Since a lot of the value of MCTS comes from aggregating over randomized rollouts, I would imagine randomization might lead to better performance. (On the other hand, the proposed "sequence caching" wouldn't work for random rollouts.)
  - This choice is also confusing from a clarity standpoint; I expected the rollouts to be sample-based given that the method was based on MCTS.
  - *The authors have rephrased this to not say their method is exactly MCTS, although I do have some remaining suggestions for how to make this clearer; see discussion.*
- The main evaluation results are based on a seemingly arbitrary set of hyperparameters for each decoding strategy, and it's not clear to me that the comparisons (e.g. in Table 1) are fair.
  - **(resolved in new revision)** As one example, their method explores only the top 3 tokens at each state, but their sample-and-filter baseline explores the top 5, and SMCG-TD doesn't have any top-k restriction (at least not stated in the paper).
  - **(resolved in comments)** Additionally, the plots in Figure 4 show much smaller differences between their method and SMCG-TD than the differences in Table 1. This suggests that the differences in Table 1 are partially explained by generating different numbers of programs, or running for different amounts of time, due to the arbitrary hyperparameters selected for comparison.
    - *The authors have included updated results in the comments below. Indeed their approach generates more programs by default. For a small budget, their approach is slightly worse than the SMCG-TD baseline, whereas for a large budget their approach is better. Their approach is also faster relative to the number of unique programs it generates.*
- The novelty of the approach seems fairly small relative to ordinary MCTS and to existing applications of it to LLMs (e.g. the PPL-MCTS approach of Chaffin et al. (2022)).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
### Clarity
The paper is fairly clearly written. However, the fact that the authors refer to the method as "MCTS" despite not having any sampling steps is a bit misleading.

One minor comment: on page 2, I'm not sure what the authors mean by "by treating programming languages as particular languages." What is a "particular language" in this context?

### Quality
As mentioned in the weaknesses section, I think that the proposed algorithm is not really MCTS due to not having any stochastic (Monte Carlo) sample evaluation procedure. Using truly random rollouts would yield a more faithful version of MCTS, and give a better signal of whether MCTS is useful for LLM program generation. (At the very least, it would be good to discuss this difference more explicitly in the paper, and perhaps only refer to the proposed method as being inspired by MCTS.)

I also have a number of concerns with the quality of the experimental results. It's not clear to me how the hyperparameters for their approach or for the baselines were selected, and some choices seem unfair. For instance, their method only considers the top 3 tokens at each step, whereas sample-and-filter uses top 5 sampling, and SMCG-TD may not use any top-k sampling. This means that their method is exploring a significantly smaller search space than all of the baselines! So if good programs exist under a top-3 restriction, their method has a much higher chance of finding them. It seems important to use the same search space for all of the baselines (i.e. use the same top-k restriction) in order to fairly compare the node-expansion strategies.

It's also hard for me to reconcile the results in Table 1 with those in Figure 4. In Table 1, PG-TD appears to often outperform SMCG-TD by a large margin. However, in Figure 4, the two methods have very similar performance at a fixed number of generated programs or at a fixed runtime. Since the hyperparameters directly affect both the number of generated programs and the accuracy of each method, it seems critical that the comparisons in Table 1 be conducted for some fixed value of these. For instance, one could select the number of generated programs for sample-and-filter and for SMCG-TD to match the number of generated programs explored by their method.

### Novelty
I have not seen any other works that uses both MCTS and large language models to do program generation. However, there are previous works that do pairwise combinations of these (e.g. MCTS with a language model, MCTS for program generation, language models for program generation), so the combination of all three is only marginally novel technically speaking.

The two caching methods proposed by the authors seem interesting and useful, although they appear to be fairly straightforward applications of memo-ization techniques rather than being totally novel ideas.

Regardless of the technical novelty, there is value in providing new empirical evidence that these techniques work well in the problem synthesis setting. However, given my concerns about the experimental results, I'm not sure the evidence is strong enough to be significant.

### Reproducibility
The paper describes their approach clearly enough that I think it could be reimplemented, although it is fairly complex so this might require a bit of effort. I think the experiments could be reimplemented as well based on the information  provided, but I'm not particularly confident the findings would be robust to slightly different hyperparameter choices or implementations.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Although combining MCTS with a LLM for program generation is a good idea, there is not much technical novelty, and I have concerns about the validity of the empirical claims and whether it is appropriate to call the proposed approach MCTS given that it removes the stochastic part. I don't think this paper currently meets the bar for acceptance.

I think this paper could be strengthened by
- investigating the behavior of the planning algorithm when rollouts are actually drawn randomly rather than via greedy search or beam search (in other words, when the planning algorithm is actually MCTS)
- being more careful about hyperparameter choices for the baselines to ensure any differences are due to the differences in action selection / exploration / planning, rather than being due to differences in search space size or generated program budgets.

**Updated review:** The authors have addressed my concerns: they have clarified the relationship to MCTS, adjusted baselines to use more similar hyperparameters, and ran a comparison of beam search to sampling-based MCTS (for which their beam search method does better). In the discussion thread below, they have also included additional comparisons for Table 1 (labeled Table F in the comments below) that give a better sense of the performance of their approach; it consistently outperforms sampling-and-filtering, and given either a fixed computation time or a large enough budget, it also seems to outperform the SMCG-TD baseline (although only by a small margin). I have updated my score from 3 to 8, with the understanding that the updated results will be included in the final version of the paper if accepted.

**Q4. Related work on using MCTS with LLMs.**
> The novelty of the approach seems fairly small relative to ordinary MCTS and to existing applications of it to LLMs (e.g. the PPL-MCTS approach of Chaìn et al. (2022)).

We have discussed other works that use MCTS and LLMs in *Planning in natural language processing* in the related work. As we have stated in the section, all these previous works use a pretrained neural network or an existing metric as a reward function. Take PPL-MCTS for example, they combine MCTS with a pre-trained discriminator instead of an LLM. The discriminator can be used to evaluate any states (partial or complete ones), which can be easily integrated with MCTS to estimate the value of a node (or state). However, in our case, the code generation LLM can only evaluate complete programs and is more expensive to run. We'll need to generate complete programs using beam search and design caching mechanisms to reduce repetitive generation calls to the LLM.

We want to again emphasize the following contributions.
1. We are the first to combine MCTS with large language models for general-purpose programming language generation. Our algorithm achieves significantly better performance than benchmarking algorithms in the literature.
2. We have designed the interfaces between these two components and dealt with the unique challenges of making the framework computationally efficient.
3. We have also demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed PG-TD for other coding targets like generating shorter codes and codes with more comments in the experiment section, and show that codes generated PG-TD can better finetune the LLM.

As the reviewer has noted, there are works that integrate MCTS with LLM for *natural language processing* tasks, which we have also discussed in our related work section. However, it remains an open and challenging problem how to effectively develop an algorithm that handles the unique challenges of code generation. For example, how to make use of the available test cases to develop a better code generation decoder. How to design an algorithm that avoids repeated computation during the search process.

> One minor comment: on page 2, I'm not sure what the authors mean by "by treating programming languages as particular languages." What is a "particular language" in this context?

We are sorry for the confusion. We meant "the Transformer treats the programming languages in the same way as natural languages." Since transformer-based language models have shown impressive capacities on natural language tasks, we can use similar transformer-based models to handle programming languages by treating programming language data as particular natural language data. We have modified the section to improve clarity.

We will revise the paper to make sure we mention it as a tree search algorithm, and also emphasize that we use beam search in the evaluation step of our tree search algorithm.

Regarding Table 1, we have some updated results below on the pass rates of different algorithms **under the same number of generated programs** (Table F). In this table, we use the APPS GPT-2 (1.5B) model as the backbone Transformer and evaluate our algorithms on the APPS introductory dataset. We essentially limit the number of function calls to the Transformer generation function so the generated programs are limited. For PG-TD and SMCG-TD, we make them stop early when the program generation budget is reached and return the best solution found so far. We still fix $k=3$, that is, only the top-3 most-likely tokens are considered for all algorithms. We report the results of PG-TD under different rollout times and beam sizes (b), and SMCG-TD under different population sizes.

Based on the results in Table F below, we have the following observations. First, both PG-TD and SMCG-TD outperform the Sampling + Filtering method. This confirms the benefit of integrating a planning or search algorithm into the Transformer beam search algorithm for code generation. Second, PG-TD finds the best program with a larger program generation budget (when the budget is 1024 or $\infty$). Particularly, PG-TD (rollout=9, b=5) has the best performance when no program generation budget is imposed. This shows our algorithm's effectiveness in searching and finding better solutions. We also notice that with a smaller number of generated programs (i.e. 512), SMCG-TD (population=100) achieves slightly better performance than our algorithm. We believe the reason is that a small program generation budget makes the tree search terminate too early. It may not have carefully searched the lower (deeper) part of the tree.


Table F. Pass rates (%) of PG-TD and other algorithms under different program generation budgets.
| Algorithm \ Program Generation Budget | 512       | 1024      | $\infty$  |
| ------------------------------ | --------- | --------- | --------- |
| PG-TD (rollout=3, b=1)         | 23.11     | 23.14     | 23.14     |
| PG-TD (rollout=3, b=3)         | 24.16     | 24.45     | 26.53     |

| PG-TD (rollout=9, b=5)         | 22.85     | 24.24     | **27.68** |
| SMCG-TD (population=50)        | 23.76     | 23.76     | 23.76     |
| SMCG-TD (population=100)       | **25.02** | 25.04     | 25.04     |
| Sampling + Filtering           | 16.75     | \-        | \-        |

| Algorithm \ Program Generation Budget | 5|
| ------------------------------ | --------- |
| Beam Search                    | 11.95     |

Also, note that **when complete programs need to be generated from the same prefix, it is only counted as one generated program because of caching**. SMCG-TD is a sampling-based algorithm and it could have a lot of identical partial programs in its population. Generating complete programs from identical partial programs would not contribute to the total number of generated programs.  Increasing its population size would indeed help increase the diversity of its population. However, it does not help much in generating more unique programs, as the number of generated programs only slightly increases when we increase the population size from 10 to 100 (Fig. 4 (left)).
PG-TD, on the other hand, would explicitly search for different unique problems by following different paths in the tree, which makes it have generally higher number of generated programs than SMCG-TD.

It may also help understand the performance of the algorithms from their computational cost perspective. As shown in Fig. 4 (right), SMCG-TD consumes similar computation as PG-TD, while it does not generate as many unique samples and has a lower pass rate than PG-TD. **Given the same computational budget, PG-TD constantly generates the best programs.**

We hope that the provided new experiments and additional explanations have convinced you of the merits of our work. Please do not hesitate to contact us if you have other concerns.

We appreciate your time! Thank you so much!

Best, Authors

* The examples of code shown are odd, in that it tends to generate unnecessarily complicated code for quite simple problems, stating `print(2*(r**2)-r**2)` instead of `print(r**2)`.
* Please discuss the failure modes, for both PG-TD and baselines, are they not compiling or failing test cases?
* I find pass rate an odd metric. These problems are simple and the input is constrained, so if the code doesn't solve them 100% then is it not incorrect code? If nothing else, the authors should report the number of tasks solved 100%. 
* The computation times are quite slow and somewhat prohibitive, perhaps an improved LLM would help with this or a smaller one to search more quickly. Can you early terminate? What if a beam achieves 100% pass rate during search, do you stop?
* The caching I do not see as a major contribution. Writing a dictionary for cache[query or partial] should suffice unless I misunderstood. 
* Though mostly clearly written, the statement of contributions, introduction, and abstract can be more clear what actually is done. What planning algorithm, what computationally efficient design mechanisms? These should be presented early and clearly for the reader.
* The method itself is reasonable interesting, integrating MCTS to the search, and it might be useful to show the approach on more varied problems, perhaps other coding challenges or BigBench benchmarks.

content.title: Response to Reviewer fkta
content.comment:
Dear Reviewer fkta,

We appreciate the reviewer for the detailed comments and insightful suggestions.

**Q1: The Codex baseline.**
> Codex for example would be a much stronger approach a minimize issues like the second sentence in the abstract “ Although the programs they generate achieve high token-matching-based scores, they often fail to compile or generate incorrect outputs.”

We agree with the reviewer that Codex indeed generates better codes than the models used in our paper. The main reason that we do not use it for experiments is that it is not open-sourced and OpenAI limits the model's API usage. We have run both beam search and PG-TD algorithms using **Codex** as the backbone. We follow the "best practices" provided in the Codex guide to put the problem description into a block comment in the beginning, and ask Codex to complete the rest. As we expect, PG-TD helps Codex generate better codes. This further validates our claim that our method is model-agnostic and can help a pre-trained code generation Transformer generate better codes.

Our results are reported in the following table. Due to the limits of the OpenAI APIs, we are only able to test the algorithms on a small set of data.

Table A. Comparison between using different Transformers as backbones for code generation, evaluated on the first 42 APPS introductory problems.

| Model       | Decoding Algorithm | Pass Rate | Strict Accuracy |
| ------------ | ---------- | --------- | --------------- |
| APPS GPT-2 (1.5B) | Beam Search | 9.38          | 0.0                |
| APPS GPT-2 (1.5B) | PG-TD | 30.99          | 2.38                |
| Codex (code-davinci-002) | Beam Search | 34.56        | 9.52                |
| Codex (code-davinci-002) | PG-TD | 47.17         | 23.80                |



**Q2. Computational Analysis.**
> The authors should report cost of running the algorithm.

Thanks for your advice. Indeed, we have reported the computational analysis in Fig. 4. In the right of Fig. 4, the computation times of the variations of PG-TD and the baseline algorithms are reported. With the same computational budget, PG-TD generates better codes than the baseline algorithms.


**Q3. About zero-shot setting and comparison with prompting baselines.**
> I believe all the results in this paper are zero-shot (or else I missed this), but presumably much of the issues would be solved with simple prompting with a few examples. The authors should compare to this.

The large language models used in our PG-TD is **not** zero-shot. Since the large language models (GPT-1.5B and GPT-Neo) were first pre-trained on massive code data and then finetuned on APPS training datasets to generate solutions to the coding problems. Note that such a setting was also used in the APPS paper [1] and AlphaCode [2]. It is a good idea to add prompting baselines for the general language models. However, **It has been reported in Table 2 of the original APPS paper [1] that a standard few-shot prompting method with GPT-3 (175B) achieves much lower pass rates than finetuning (0.55 vs 10.15).** This also confirms the necessity to use the proposed PG-TD with a *finetuned* transformer to achieve good performance.

[1]. Dan Hendrycks, Steven Basart, Saurav Kadavath, Mantas Mazeika, Akul Arora, Ethan Guo, Collin Burns, Samir Puranik, Horace He, Dawn Song, and Jacob Steinhardt. Measuring coding challenge competence with APPS. NeurIPS, 2021.

[2]. Yujia Li, David Choi, Junyoung Chung, Nate Kushman, Julian Schrittwieser, R ́emi Leblond, Tom Eccles, James Keeling, Felix Gimeno, and Agustin Dal Lago. Competition-Level Code Generation with AlphaCode. arXiv preprint arXiv:2203.07814, 2022.


**Q4: About failure modes.**
> Please discuss the failure modes, for both PG-TD and baselines, are they not compiling or failing test cases?

In the table below, we report the average percentages of test cases where compilation errors and runtime errors occur. We use the error analysis utility provided in the original APPS codebase. As we expect, PG-TD executes the generated programs and finds the ones with higher pass rates, so it dramatically reduces the percentage of both types of errors.


Table C. Failure case analysis. The percentages are averaged over the APPS introductory dataset.
|                                | Compilation Error (%) | Runtime Error (%) |
| ------------------------------ | --------------------- | ----------------- |
| APPS GPT-2 (1.5B), Beam Search | 5.58                  | 32.95             |
| APPS GPT-2 (1.5B), Sampling + Filtering    | 4.68                  | 27.38                  |
| APPS GPT-2 (1.5B), PG-TD       | 1.93                  | 19.50             |

content.comment:
**Q5: On evaluation metrics.**
> I find pass rate an odd metric. These problems are simple and the input is constrained, so if the code doesn't solve them 100% then is it not incorrect code? If nothing else, the authors should report the number of tasks solved 100%.

Thanks for your suggestion on reporting percentages of problems in which code-generation algorithms pass all test cases. Indeed, this is the **strict accuracy** metric we used in the experiment sections (Table 1). We use pass rates as rewards as they provide more dense signals than strict accuracies. However, we do find that the generated programs with higher pass rates also tend to achieve higher strict accuracies.


**Q6: About termination conditions.**
> The computation times are quite slow and somewhat prohibitive, perhaps an improved LLM would help with this or a smaller one to search more quickly. Can you early terminate? What if a beam achieves 100% pass rate during search, do you stop?

We agree that early terminating when finding a solution with a pass rate of 1 would certainly make our algorithms more efficient. In the table below, we find enabling early termination does improve the algorithms' computational efficiencies. We will include this implementation choice in the paper. We expect early termination would be more helpful when the code generation algorithms can solve most of the problems (achieving pass rates of 1 on most of them), which is not the case for the current model.

Table D. Computation times with and without early stopping, using APPS GPT-2 (1.5B).
|                                                  | Computation Time (sec.) |
| ------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------- |
| PG-TD without early termination (as in paper)    | 1177.99                        |
| PG-TD with early termination                     | 986.37                        |
| Sampling without early termination (as in paper) | 2154.23                        |
| Sampling with early termination                  | 2081.25                        |

On the other hand, for n@k metrics (reported in Table 6), the code-generation agent may not want to terminate early. Under these metrics, the agent can submit multiple solutions and be considered as solving the problem if any of the submitted solutions passes all the **private** test cases. The agent can benefit from finding multiple solutions that pass all the **public** test cases and submit all of them for evaluation.

**Q7. Caching algorithms.**
> The caching I do not see as a major contribution. Writing a dictionary for cache[query or partial] should suìce unless I misunderstood.


We find that **simply caching all the generated sequences and reusing them later would not be sufficient**. In *sequence caching*, we do cache all the generated sequences. These sequences can be reused in the evaluation step in MCTS when we need to generate complete programs from partial programs. Importantly, we justified that reusing the cached sequences are greedily-optimal when the beam size is 1, and the cached sequences may not be greedily-optimal (that is, the cached sequences can be different from the sequences generated by rerunning the beam search algorithm) when the beam size is larger than 1. We have more detailed discussions in Sec. C.2.

We also contributed to designing *tree structure caching* by identifying the tree structure shared by the Transformer and MCTS, so that the most-likely next tokens of partial programs found by the beam search algorithm can be shared with MCTS for building the tree later. This method is unique to combining MCTS with beam search, and to the best of our knowledge, how this combination can be made more efficient is not addressed in the literature.

content.comment:
In this discussion period, we have the following new results and revisions to the paper.
* **Results on Codex** (Reviewer fkta, FcyD). The reviewers have raised the question that our paper does not use the most capable code-generation Transformer (for example, OpenAI Codex). The main reason is that Codex is **not open-sourced** and OpenAI limits the frequency of calling their code generation APIs (20 times per second). So we cannot conduct large-scale experiments using the Codex model. In this rebuttal, we strive to perform more experiments using Codex as the backbone code-generation Transformer and generating codes using beam search vs. PG-TD. We are able to perform the comparison on a subset of APPS problems and are still able to find that **using Codex, PG-TD generates much higher-quality codes compared with using beam search**. This result further confirms that our algorithm is model-agnostic.

Table A. Comparisons between using different Transformers as backbones for code generation, evaluated on the first 42 APPS introductory problems.

| Model       | Decoding Algorithm | Pass Rate | Strict Accuracy |
| ------------ | ---------- | --------- | --------------- |
| APPS GPT-2 (1.5B) | Beam Search | 9.38          | 0.0                |
| APPS GPT-2 (1.5B) | PG-TD | 30.99          | 2.38                |
| Codex (code-davinci-002) | Beam Search | 34.56        | 9.52                |
| Codex (code-davinci-002) | PG-TD | 47.17         | 23.80                |

* **Sampling-based MCTS** (Reviewer kmKW). In the evaluation step of our MCTS algorithm, we generate greedily-optimal solutions from a partial program using beam search. We could instead use a sampling approach, which would be a more faithful implementation of MCTS as suggested by the reviewer. We experimented with using sampling in the generation step and found that **using beam search in the evaluation step of the tree search algorithm does have a better performance than using sampling**.

Table B. PG-TD using beam search vs. sampling in the evaluation step, evaluated on the first 500 APPS introductory problems.
| Decoding Algorithm     | Pass Rate | Strict Accuracy |
| ---------------------- | --------- | --------------- |
| PG-TD using Beam Search (as in paper) | 32.757          | 13.20                |
| PG-TD using Sampling | 15.69          | 5.0                |

* **Consistent baseline hyper-parameters** (Reviewer kmKW). In the experiments in our original submission, we use top-k sampling where k=5, hoping this benefits sampling. For other experiments, we use k=3. We now set k=3 for both our algorithms and the baseline algorithms, that is, only the first three most-likely tokens are considered in each generation step (except when we explicitly change the tree width in the variations of PG-TD in Fig. 4). We have updated Fig. 4 to reflect the change.
* **Algorithm failure mode analysis** (Reviewr fkta). We have re-evaluated the generation solutions and reported the types of errors when the generated programs fail to run. As we expect, PG-TD has a lower error rate compared with other baseline algorithms in terms of both compilation error and runtime error.

Table C. Failure case analysis. The percentages are averaged over the APPS introductory dataset.
|                                | Compilation Error (%) | Runtime Error (%) |
| ------------------------------ | --------------------- | ----------------- |
| APPS GPT-2 (1.5B), Beam Search | 5.58                  | 32.95             |
| APPS GPT-2 (1.5B), Sampling + Filtering    | 4.68                  | 27.38                  |
| APPS GPT-2 (1.5B), PG-TD       | 1.93                  | 19.50             |
* **More description of the MCTS algorithm in the main paper** (Reviewer Xzif, FcyD). We have summarized the description of the MCTS algorithm in the main paper so that readers do not need to refer to the appendix to understand the basics of the algorithm.
* **Qualitative analysis** (Reviewer fkta, FcyD). The examples we show in the paper are indeed easy problems where APPS GPT-2 Transformers fail. We added a new example where **the Codex model fails to solve the problem using beam search, but successfully solves the problem (pass rate = 1) using PG-TD**. We include the example in Fig. 15 in the revision.

Please see our detailed responses to all the reviewers below.

content.title: General Response to All Reviewers
content.comment:
We thank all the reviewers for taking time to review our paper and providing insightful feedback. We are glad that reviewers recognized the following contributions.
* **Task**. The task we consider in this paper is important and has a broad interest.

> The paper approaches an important research area. (Reviewer fkta)

> This is an interesting direction, focusing on a core part of neural code generation that often receives little attention. (Reviewer Xzif)

> The problem is important and has a broad interest. (Reviewer FcyD)

* **Method**. Our approach of integrating LLM with MCTS for code generation is novel and reasonable.

> The idea of treating code generation as an RL problem, where input-output pairs provide the reward, is novel and related to much work in program synthesis. (Reviewer FcyD)

> Integrating LM generation with MCTS is a good idea, allowing the search process to focus on prefixes with a higher chance of producing good programs. (Reviewer kmKW)

> The paper approaches an important research area, improving generation for LLMs and proposes a reasonable approach for it that does not require any additional training and minimal code complexity. (Reviewer fkta) 

* **Experiment**. We show empirical evidence that our method significantly outperforms baseline algorithms.

> The results demonstrate it outperforms baselines in performance. (Reviewer fkta)

> The empirical results indicate a significant improvement over baselines for the evaluated models. (Reviewer Xzif)

> Their method seems to slightly outperform baseline methods given a fixed runtime budget, without needing to retrain the transformer model. (Reviewer kmKW)


**Novelty.** 
First, we **never claim** the application of MCTS in neural program synthesis is our main contribution (as discussed in the related work section). Instead, our work aims to answer the question **if MCTS can be integrated with large language models (models at the scale of ~2B parameters, and Codex in our new results with ~12B parameters) for competitive-level code generation, and if the Transformer + MCTS framework outperforms the well-accepted Sampling + Filtering scheme that has shown successes in the literature (used by AlphaCode, etc.).** To this end, we propose concrete designs of the framework to achieve strong performance (how the information provided by the Transformer should be used by MCTS, and using beam search in the evaluation step instead of using the standard sampling method, etc.), as well as improve the efficiency of the overall framework (the caching methods).

We also want to emphasize that our proposed algorithm, PG-TD, is **model-agnostic**. The goal is not to use an extremely large model (with sufficient training data) to achieve state-of-out-art performance in code generation. Our work focuses on the following problem. **Given a pre-trained code-generation model (which could have a small size or does not perform perfectly on a dataset), can we improve its performance by only changing the decoding method with the help of some test cases**, without necessarily increasing the size of the model, finetuning the model, and using more human-written sample solutions as training data?

We emphasize our contributions as follows.
1. We are the first to combine MCTS with large language models for general-purpose programming language generation from natural language descriptions. Our algorithm achieves a significantly better performance than the existing well-accepted baselines. Reviewer kmKW has recognized the empirical value of showing that MCTS works well with LLM for code generation. 
2. We have designed the interfaces between the MCTS and LLM and dealt with the unique challenges of making the framework computationally efficient.
3. We demonstrated the versatility of PG-TD by optimizing other coding targets like generating shorter codes and codes with more comments (Fig. 5 in paper), and also showed that codes generated by PG-TD can help further finetune the code-generation Transformer, achieving a self-learning framework without requiring extra human-written training samples (Table 4 in paper).

content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn:
Strengths: This is an interesting direction, focusing on a core part of neural code generation that often receives little attention.
The empirical results indicate a significant improvement over baselines for the evaluated models.  The idea of treating code generation as an RL problem, where input-output pairs provide the reward, is novel and relevant to much work in program synthesis. The authors response was strong and addressed many of the weaknesses.

Weaknesses: The main weakness was seen to be the use of both an English description of the task to be solved as well as a set of unit tests (input/output pairs).  Writing code with both a natural language language description and provided unit tests seems a poor match to actual coding, or at least a less challenging problem that working from English alone.

In the end it was decided that this paper is working in an established paradigm and within that paradigm it is a fairly complete paper and would not benefit greatly from another revision.  One reviewer would still like to see a demonstration of generating unit tests from natural language descriptions as was claimed to be possible in an author response.
